citations.authority: Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc. (short form)
citations.cited_for: A dispute is genuine only if a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the nonmoving party.

citations.cited_for: Injured party has an affirmative duty to take reasonable steps to minimize damages.
citations.context: Under both Georgia common law and the Restatement (Second) of Contracts, an injured party has an affirmative duty to take reasonable steps to minimize its damages. See O.C.G.A. § 13-6-8; Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 350 (1981).

first_check.explanation: O.C.G.A. § 13-6-8 governs remote or consequential damages, not mitigation. Georgia's contract duty to mitigate is O.C.G.A. § 13-6-5, which binds an injured party to lessen damages as far as practicable by ordinary care and diligence. That supports the stated proposition. The memo's Table of Authorities mislabels § 13-6-8 as 'Duty to Mitigate.' The companion cite to Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 350 was not checked here.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: § 13-6-8: "Remote or consequential damages are not recoverable unless they can be traced solely to the breach of the contract or unless they are capable of exact computation..." § 13-6-5: "Where by a breach of contract a party is injured, he is bound to lessen the damages as far as is practicable by the use of ordinary care and diligence."

second_check.explanation: Finding holds. O.C.G.A. § 13-6-8 reads: 'Remote or consequential damages are not recoverable unless they can be traced solely to the breach of the contract or unless they are capable of exact computation...' It says nothing about mitigation. The duty to mitigate is O.C.G.A. § 13-6-5: 'Where by a breach of contract a party is injured, he is bound to lessen the damages as far as is practicable by the use of ordinary care and diligence.' The proposition is correct, but the section number is wrong.

citations.cited_for: Injured party has affirmative duty to take reasonable steps to minimize damages (avoidability).

Strictly, § 350 is a limit on damages rather than a duty, but it supports the memo's next sentence, 'Damages that could have been avoided ... are not recoverable.' Text read as quoted by the Nebraska Supreme Court and Florida DCA; the Restatement itself is not freely available.

first_check.evidence_excerpt: § 13-6-8: "Remote or consequential damages are not recoverable unless they can be traced solely to the breach of the contract..." § 13-6-5: "he is bound to lessen the damages as far as is practicable by the use of ordinary care and diligence."

second_check.explanation: Finding holds. I read O.C.G.A. § 13-6-8, and it covers remote and consequential damages, not mitigation. Verbatim: "Remote or consequential damages are not recoverable unless they can be traced solely to the breach of the contract or unless they are capable of exact computation..." The mitigation duty is in § 13-6-5: "Where by a breach of contract a party is injured, he is bound to lessen the damages as far as is practicable by the use of ordinary care and diligence." The proposition is a correct statement of Georgia law, but it is attached to the wrong section number. The correct cite is O.C.G.A. § 13-6-5.

This check covers only what the statute says.

citations.cited_for: Plaintiff's recovery reduced in proportion to its fault; plaintiff 50 percent or more at fault is barred.
citations.context: Under Georgia's modified comparative fault statute, O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, a plaintiff's recovery is reduced in proportion to its percentage of fault, and a plaintiff whose fault equals or exceeds 50 percent is barred from recovery altogether.

That scope issue is a matter of argument, not a misstatement of the statute's text.
